source: Aquinas, Summa Theologica I.2.3 (First Way, condensed)
text: Some things in the world are in motion. Whatever is in motion is put in motion by something else, since nothing can move itself from potentiality to actuality except by something already actual. This chain of movers cannot regress infinitely, because without a first mover there would be no subsequent motion at all. Therefore there must exist a first, unmoved mover, which everyone understands to be God.

label.conclusion: There must exist a first, unmoved mover, which everyone understands to be God.
premises: Some things in the world are in motion.

source: Aquinas, Summa Theologica I.2.3 (Second Way, condensed)
text: In the world we observe an order of efficient causes. Nothing can be the efficient cause of itself, for that would mean it existed before itself, which is impossible. Causes cannot regress infinitely, since removing the first cause removes all the intermediate and final causes. Therefore there must be a first efficient cause, which we call God.

label.conclusion: There must be a first efficient cause, which we call God.
premises: We observe an order of efficient causes in the world.
Nothing can be the efficient cause of itself.

source: Aquinas, Summa Theologica I.2.3 (Fifth Way / teleological, condensed)
text: We observe that natural bodies lacking intelligence, such as plants and animals, nevertheless act toward an end in a regular way, always or nearly always achieving the best result. Things without intelligence cannot tend toward an end unless directed by something with knowledge and intelligence, as an arrow is directed by an archer. Therefore some intelligent being exists that directs all natural things to their end, and this we call God.

text: Either God exists or God does not exist, and reason alone cannot settle the matter. If you wager that God exists and you are right, you gain infinite happiness; if you are wrong, you lose little. If you wager that God does not exist and you are wrong, you risk infinite loss; if you are right, you gain little. Given the possibility of infinite gain against finite loss, it is rational to wager that God exists.

label.conclusion: It is rational to wager that God exists.

Therefore God must exist in reality and not merely in the understanding.

Therefore, either God is not omnipotent, not benevolent, or God does not exist as traditionally conceived.

text: Consider whether the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious, or whether it is pious because it is loved by the gods. If the gods love it because it is already pious, then piety must be something independent of their approval, and their love merely tracks an external standard. If instead it is pious only because the gods love it, then piety has no fixed nature of its own and could change if the gods' preferences changed. Either way, defining piety simply as 'what the gods love' fails to explain what piety actually is.

label.conclusion: Defining piety simply as 'what the gods love' fails to explain what piety actually is.

text: I can doubt the existence of my body, the external world, and even mathematical truths, since a deceiving demon might be misleading me about all of these. Therefore, I exist, at least as a thinking thing.

label.conclusion: I exist, at least as a thinking thing.

Therefore, our confidence that the future will resemble the past cannot be rationally justified by argument; it rests on habit rather than reason.
